newsitem.title: MOZAMBIQUE: Mozambican bosses and workers united on cashews.
newsitem.headline: Mozambican bosses and workers united on cashews.

text.p: In a rare display of solidarity, the owners and workers of Mozambique's cashew factories have joined forces to accuse the government and the World Bank of bringing the industry to the brink of ruin.

At a seminar in Maputo this week employers and trade union representatives have blasted the Maputo government for bowing to the World Bank's demand for an end to protection for the industry, traditionally a major exporter.
The Association of Cashew Processing Industries (AICAJU) on Wednesday accused the government of deceit, and of imposing, in partnership with the Bank, "ruinous conditions" on the industry.

Presenting the industry's point of view at the seminar AICAJU chairman Kekobad Patel said privatisation would never have happened if the businessmen had known in advance that the government planned to strip the industry of protection.
The issue which unites the industrialists and the Cashew Workers Union (SINTIC) against the government and the World Bank is the liberalisation of the trade in unprocessed nuts.
This decision, taken after privatisation, is blamed for depriving the industry of raw material. The privatised factories are unable to compete with traders who are exporting unshelled nuts to India.
Protection had been via a surtax on the export of unshelled nuts. This started out at 26 per cent in 1995, but, under World Bank pressure was cut to 20 per cent in 1996.
For 1997, the World Bank had demanded a cutback to 12 per cent. The government cut the surtax to 14 per cent.
Patel thought this concession to the industry was meaningless. He said: "Twelve percent or 14 percent, it's all the same. It's ruinous for the industry.

The SINTIC General Secretary, Boaventura Mondlane, distributed to the seminar a letter he had sent to Oldemiro Baloi, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Tourism, in May, expressing his concern at the closure of a processing plant.
Mondlane had asked the government to suspend the export of raw nuts, or at least raise the surtax back to 20 per cent, and to ensure that the industry was not starved of raw materials.
More than two months have passed, and the government has not replied to Mondlane's letter, he said.
In 1994, immediately prior to privatisation, all six of the state-owned cashew factories were at a standstill. Only two private companies were operational then.
With privatisation, and injections of fresh capital, the factories began to operate again.
Prospects for the sector looked bright. Millions of dollars went into rehabilitating some private factories that had been paralysed for years.

From just two operational factories and 4,000 workers -- many of whom had been laid off for several years on 60 per cent of their wages -- the sector grew to 16 operational plants employing 8,000 workers.

"But once privatisation was complete, the government, together with the World Bank, completely changed the policy it had been following, which was to ensure supplies of nuts for the factories as the top priority," Patel said.
Instead trade was fully liberalised, and the export of raw nuts was prioritised, he added.
The result was clear to see -- two factories had already shut down because of shortages of raw material, and a third will follow later this month -- a total loss of around 2,700 jobs.
